newsitem.title: USA: Support for Medicare means test appears to grow.
newsitem.headline: Support for Medicare means test appears to grow.

text.p: President Clinton inched toward congressional Republicans Wednesday on a politically sensitive plan to boost Medicare premiums for the well-off, as both sides prepared for final balanced-budget talks.
During a news conference in Madrid, Spain, Clinton said he was willing to consider a Senate-passed plan to make well-off seniors pay higher Medicare premiums for doctor's care.

The White House previously said means testing, whereby benefits are based on the wealth of the recipients, should be considered as part of long-term Medicare reform, not the five-year budget legislation currently under discussion.
"I have never been opposed to means testing Medicare," Clinton told reporters. "If we're going to means test benefits, then means testing needs to be fair and workable."
The president does not support a companion Senate plan to raise the Medicare's eligibility age to 67 from the current 65, worried it could increase the ranks of the uninsured.

White House aides said Clinton wanted key changes in the Senate proposal to make it easier to enforce and ensure that wealthier, healthier seniors did not have a financial incentive to opt out of Medicare.
House and Senate negotiators begin meeting this week to work out compromise bill to implement a five-year balanced budget deal with the White House.

The Senate version of the bill forces seniors with higher incomes to pay higher premiums for Medicare Part B, covering doctor's care. The government now subsidises 75 percent of the premium, beneficiaries pay 25 percent. The premium would be $540 next year when the legislation would take effect.

Under the Senate bill, seniors making $50,000 or more and couples making $75,000 and above would face higher bills. The premium would rise to a maximum of $2,160 for couples making $125,000 and individuals making more than $100,000.
The House did not include the means test, estimated to save $3.9 billion over five years, in its budget legislation.

Many House Republicans are still reeling from the 1996 elections when Democrats accused them of trying to gut Medicare. They voted for means testing as part of a failed 1995 budget bill but are holding back now, hoping for political cover from Clinton.

California Republican Representative William Thomas, chairman of a House subcommittee that oversees Medicare, complained Clinton refused to take a firm stance. He said Clinton's position seemed to be that he "may possibly, quite likely, if everything was right ... think it was a good idea."

White House officials wanted to make sure they do not jeopardise passage of the budget bill or alienate House Democrats, many of whom opposed the Medicare change. House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt opposed the plan, though Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle was open to it.
Clinton wanted the Senate bill changed to ensure that even the wealthiest seniors would not have to pay 100 percent of the premium, fearing they might leave Medicare.
The White House wanted the means test administered by the Treasury Department, not the Department of Health and Human Services. They said HHS involvement was too unwieldly and expensive.

The nation's largest senior citizen's group, the American Association of Retired Persons, was spending millions of dollars on a grassroots campaign to defeat the proposed increase in the eligibility age and other Medicare provisions, but was not mobilising the troops on the premium issue.

"We do not see this as an issue of principle, but rather one of practicality. The issues are the administrative enforcement and also whether the principle would be applied to other programmes beyond Medicare," said John Rother of the AARP.
